strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use a trust-region sequential linear-programming search that keeps the original nonsmooth maximum over all finite-support lags. At each feasible iterate, form the exact first-order affine model of every lag sum and solve a linear epigraph problem over a bounded, mass-preserving step. Adapt the step radius using the exact evaluator score: accept only an actually improving feasible candidate, shrink after rejection or poor agreement, and cautiously enlarge after a strong improvement. Use seeded feasible restarts around the supplied construction, then retain the best candidate by exact score.

This is materially different from both the supplied program and the preceding strategy. The supplied program applies SLSQP to the original nonlinear epigraph constraints and then uses a small discrete pairwise polish. The preceding strategy uses projected gradient descent on a log-sum-exp smoothing of the maximum. This plan uses neither a nonlinear constrained optimizer, smoothing, nor pairwise grid search; its primary step is an explicitly formulated LP over all affine lag models, followed by exact-score acceptance.

Facts: the evaluator’s score is a maximum of 2n−1 finite-support quadratic lag sums; the mass-and-box feasible set is convex; and the supplied SLSQP construction achieved a score near 0.380992. The LP subproblem below is a convex optimization problem supported by SciPy’s HiGHS linear-programming solver. The hypothesis is that the local LP model and exact trust-region acceptance may make useful progress while avoiding nonlinear epigraph solver difficulties, and that perturbation restarts may reach a better basin. These are search heuristics, not measured improvements. The original objective remains nonconvex, the LP is only a local model, and there is no global-optimality or 0.3808 guarantee.

2. Mathematical specification

For the runtime-selected integer n, use h ∈ Rⁿ, dx = 2/n, and s = n/2. The feasible set is K = {h : 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 1 for every i, and sum_i h[i] = s}. The samples are continuous-valued, so s is feasible also for odd n.

For each signed lag d ∈ {−n+1, …, n−1}, define I_d by lo_d = max(0,−d), hi_d = min(n,n−d), and I_d = {i : lo_d ≤ i < hi_d}. Define the raw lag sum F_d(h) = sum over i in I_d of h[i]·(1−h[i+d]). Let M(h) = max_d F_d(h). The authoritative score is C(h) = (2/n)M(h), calculated in the program as max(np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full'))·(2.0/n). The indexed F_d values are exactly the same finite-overlap lag values as that full correlation, possibly in reversed order; taking the maximum is unchanged. Include every signed lag and its partial boundary overlap. Do not use circular correlation or replace the score by one minus an autocorrelation extremum.

The derivative of a lag sum with respect to coordinate h[r] is
G[d,r] = 1{r ∈ I_d}·(1−h[r+d]) − 1{r−d ∈ I_d}·h[r−d].
For d = 0, this is 1−2h[r]. For a feasible step δ, exact expansion gives
F_d(h+δ) = F_d(h) + G[d,:]·δ − sum over i in I_d of δ[i]·δ[i+d].
If ||δ||∞ ≤ r, the absolute remainder is at most |I_d|r² ≤ nr². Thus F_d(h)+G[d,:]·δ+nr² is a valid upper bound on that lag throughout the trust box. The common constant nr² does not change which δ minimizes the maximum of these upper bounds, so it can be omitted from the LP objective and constraints; exact scoring still determines acceptance.

At a current feasible h and radius r, solve the following LP with variables δ ∈ Rⁿ and t ∈ R:
minimize t;
F_d(h) + G[d,:]·δ ≤ t for every signed d;
sum_i δ[i] = 0;
max(−r,−h[i]) ≤ δ[i] ≤ min(r,1−h[i]) for each i;
t is unbounded above and below.
The step bounds and equality make h+δ feasible and keep it in the trust box. In matrix form, each inequality row is [G[d,:], −1] with right-hand side −F_d; the equality row is [ones(n), 0] with right-hand side 0. This is a supported linear program, not a claim that the original quadratic minimax problem is convex. Compare every resulting candidate using the exact score.

For repairing arbitrary finite vectors to K, use the Euclidean projection P_K(z)[i] = clip(z[i]−λ, 0, 1), where λ is chosen so the entries sum to s. This is the joint projection onto the capped simplex; do not clip and then rescale.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Program structure and runtime inputs. Write one complete program defining run(seed=42, **kwargs) and all helper functions at top level, with no closures or lambdas. Import NumPy and scipy.optimize.linprog; no CVXPY formulation or nonlinear optimizer is needed. Use float64 throughout and a seeded NumPy random generator. Ignore unknown kwargs and perform all validation, optimization, scoring, and fallback selection inside run or its top-level helpers. Do not change resolution: the chosen n is the parent length when a usable-length parent is supplied, so no interpolation or resolution transfer is needed.

Read initial_h_values inside a guarded block using the pre-imported global, convert it to a flattened float64 array, and use its length as n if 1 ≤ length ≤ 999. If this length is valid but some entries are nonfinite, retain that n but regard the parent as unusable and use a uniform fallback. If no valid-length parent exists, parse kwargs.get('n_points', 47), convert safely to an integer, and clamp to [1,999], falling back to 47 on conversion failure. Do not override a valid parent length with n_points. Convert seed safely to an integer and use a nonnegative seed such as seed modulo 2³²; use 42 if conversion fails.

If the selected-length parent is finite, use its supplied values as the primary construction and pass them through the joint projection below. The projected vector is the feasible parent candidate and fallback, including when the supplied finite parent has a small box or mass error. If it is nonfinite or cannot be projected, use h[i]=0.5 as the fallback. A valid parent’s feasible form must remain stored separately and must never be displaced by a worse search result.

3.2. Implement capped-simplex projection. Make a top-level helper accepting a one-dimensional length-n vector. Return failure for the wrong shape or nonfinite entries. To protect the threshold calculation from extreme finite inputs, clip z to a large finite interval such as [−1e12,1e12]. Set the bisection lower threshold to min(z)−1 and upper threshold to max(z). At each midpoint λ, compute sum(clip(z−λ,0,1)); if that sum exceeds s, move the lower threshold up, otherwise move the upper threshold down. Perform up to 100 iterations, stopping early if the midpoint no longer changes.

Form h=clip(z−λ,0,1) at the final midpoint. Correct residual q=s−sum(h) jointly with the bounds: if q>0, add q in proportion to capacities 1−h[i]; if q<0, remove −q in proportion to capacities h[i]. Then correct any remaining floating-point residual by adjusting a coordinate with sufficient slack, repeating only a bounded number of times. These operations preserve the box because the requested adjustment does not exceed total available capacity. Do not subsequently clip a corrected vector in a way that can undo its mass constraint. Return failure if the result is nonfinite, outside [0,1] beyond a small numerical tolerance, or has a mass error larger than 1e−9·max(1,n).

For LP output, make a separate top-level step-repair helper. Compute the coordinate lower and upper step bounds from h and r, clip the solver’s δ to those bounds, and restore sum(δ)=0 by distributing the residual over the available upper or lower step slack. Use a proportional slack adjustment and then a bounded largest-slack correction for roundoff. Reject if mass cannot be restored or the step is nonfinite. Form h+δ and pass it through the capped-simplex projection for final feasibility; reject it if projection changes any coordinate by more than r+1e−8, so the repaired candidate still respects the trust box to numerical tolerance.

3.3. Implement exact scoring and lag derivatives. Make exact_score(h,n) reject a wrong shape, nonfinite values, box violations beyond a tight tolerance, or a sum error above a stated numerical tolerance such as 1e−8·max(1,n). For a valid vector, compute and return exactly float(max(np.correlate(h, 1.0-h, mode='full'))*(2.0/n)); otherwise return infinity. Do not return an LP model value as a score.

Make a lag helper that, for d from −n+1 through n−1, computes lo=max(0,−d), hi=min(n,n−d), row=d+n−1, and F[row]=dot(h[lo:hi], 1−h[lo+d:hi+d]). For the LP-enabled dimensions, allocate a float64 gradient matrix G of shape (2n−1,n). For each row, add 1−h[lo+d:hi+d] to G[row,lo:hi] and subtract h[lo:hi] from G[row,lo+d:hi+d]. These slice updates implement the stated derivative, including both contributions when d=0. Reject nonfinite F or G. The optimizer may use max(F) and G for its local model, but all candidate acceptance and final selection use exact_score.

3.4. Build feasible starts. Add a top-level helper that projects each proposed vector, rejects failed projections, and deduplicates against existing starts when max absolute coordinate difference is below 1e−8. Always put the fallback first.

With a finite parent, add its reversal, its complement 1−h, a deterministic np.roll shift such as n//3, and seeded Gaussian perturbations at standard deviations 0.04 and 0.10; also offer one seeded uniform-random vector if the start limit permits. Reversal and complement are feasible score symmetries at mass n/2, but include them only as starts, not as a reason to alter the evaluator. A roll is merely a start construction and is not an objective symmetry because the evaluator has finite boundaries. Project each proposal.

Without a usable parent, offer the uniform fallback, a half-block with floor(n/2) entries equal to 1 and, if n is odd, one entry equal to 0.5, an alternating 0/1 vector, the compact sinusoidal vectors 0.5+0.45·cos(2πk i/n) for k=1 and k=2, and seeded uniform-random vectors. Project all proposals, deduplicate them, exact-score them, and retain no more than the configured number of starts. These are algorithmic constructions, not copied numeric tables.

3.5. Implement one trust-region LP local search. Give a top-level helper an already projected start, n, the iteration limit, and the current global best vector and score. Reproject the start, exact-score it, and store a copy in the global best if it improves that score by more than 1e−12. Initialize the current radius to 0.08, with minimum 1e−5 and maximum 0.25.

At each local iteration, compute F and G at the current h. Build the LP with n+1 variables, one inequality for each of the 2n−1 signed lags, one equality for sum(δ)=0, the coordinate bounds specified in section 2, and an unbounded t. Call scipy.optimize.linprog with method='highs', a finite solver iteration limit such as 200, presolve enabled, and primal and dual feasibility tolerances around 1e−8. The objective coefficient vector is zero for all δ coordinates and one for t. Do not form a nonlinear SLSQP problem. If the call raises, reports failure, has the wrong result shape, or returns nonfinite values, halve r and continue to the next outer iteration; stop if r falls below its minimum.

Repair the returned δ as in section 3.2 and form the feasible projected trial. If repair fails, reject and halve r. Compute the model maximum m_lin=max_d(F_d+G[d,:]·δ), the predicted raw decrease p=max(F)−m_lin, and the trial’s exact C5 score. If the feasible trial score is less than the current exact score by more than 1e−12, accept it as the new local iterate. Update the global best only if its exact score improves the stored global score by more than 1e−12, storing a copy.

For an accepted step with p>1e−14, define rho=(current_score−trial_score)/((2/n)·p); otherwise regard rho as poor. If rho≥0.75 and max(abs(δ))≥0.8r, set r=min(0.25,1.5r). If rho<0.25, set r=max(1e−5,0.5r). Otherwise keep r unchanged. If the exact score does not improve, reject the step and halve r. Stop the local run if r<1e−5 or the projected step has max absolute size below 1e−8. Every iteration makes at most one LP call, so the run has a fixed finite solver-call bound. This is a local heuristic: neither the linearized model nor a successful LP certifies improvement in the original objective; exact acceptance is mandatory.

3.6. Orchestrate bounded searches. Exact-score the fallback first and initialize the global best from it. Exact-score every retained start and update the global best only with a feasible lower-scoring vector. Run the local LP search separately from each retained start, carrying the same global best through the runs. Isolate exceptions per start so a failure cannot erase a previously stored candidate.

After the initial starts, make a fixed number of basin-hop proposals centered on the latest global best. For n≤128, use two seeded Gaussian perturbations with standard deviations 0.025 and 0.08; for 129≤n≤256, use one perturbation with standard deviation 0.05. Project, exact-score, and locally optimize each proposal. A successful hop becomes the center for the next one. These loops execute within the generated program; they do not depend on external experimentation or feedback.

3.7. Finalize and return. Project the global best once more, validate shape, finiteness, bounds, and mass, and recompute its exact score with np.correlate. If it is invalid or has a worse score than the saved fallback, use the fallback and recompute. If the fallback is invalid, project the uniform vector and use it. Return a one-dimensional float64 h_values array, a Python float c5_bound computed from that exact returned vector, and int(n). Never return an unprojected LP step, an unscored proposal, or a surrogate score.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use the following complete defaults. For n≤64, retain up to 7 starts and allow 30 LP iterations per local run. For 65≤n≤128, retain up to 5 starts and allow 20 iterations. For 129≤n≤256, retain up to 2 starts and allow 8 iterations. For n>256, skip LP local search and use the feasible fallback plus any bounded feasible starts that fit the start limit; exact-score those candidates and return the best. The n>256 rule bounds dense LP work on a single CPU while preserving a valid return for every allowed resolution. Use the basin-hop counts and noise scales in section 3.6. The supplied n=47 construction therefore uses the small-dimension defaults.

Safely parse kwargs.starts as an override clamped to 1..8 and kwargs.max_iter as an override clamped to 0..60; invalid values use the dimension-based defaults. max_iter is per local run, not a total shared budget. For n>256, keep LP search disabled even if max_iter was supplied. Use the trust-radius defaults, growth and shrink factors, score-improvement tolerance, and stopping rules in section 3.5. Use the HiGHS LP settings stated there. Ignore unknown kwargs.

Correctness requirements are fixed: select the parent length when valid, keep n≤999, include every signed finite-support lag, enforce both box and mass constraints jointly, use an LP only for the explicitly stated affine model, exact-score every candidate that may be selected, preserve the fallback, and return the exact evaluator score. A coder may vary the starting radius within about 0.04–0.12, the maximum radius within 0.15–0.35, the number of small-n starts within 4–8, or small-n LP iterations within 15–45. Any such choice must remain bounded in the program and retain exact-score acceptance. Do not describe a parameter choice as experimentally optimal.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 and reject nonfinite inputs and proposals. Projection clips extreme finite proposal magnitudes before bisection; mass correction uses available box slack. The final candidate is reprojected and revalidated. The exact evaluator has finite products for feasible h. Build the gradient by slice accumulation and never form a Hessian or a quadratic-program matrix.

The LP gradient and inequality arrays use O(n²) storage only when n≤256; at n=256, G has 511×256 entries, about 1.1 MB in float64, plus a similarly sized LP constraint array and solver overhead. At n>256, skip this construction. Exact full correlation uses O(n) output memory and at most O(n²) work; n is capped at 999. Execute sequentially on the one available CPU, with no parallel work. The start, iteration, and radius limits make all optimization loops finite.

Treat an LP exception, unsuccessful status, infeasible-looking or nonfinite result, failed repair, or rejected exact-score proposal as a failed step, not as a program-wide failure. Halve the radius as specified and retain the best candidate already stored. Termination occurs at the iteration budget, minimum radius, or small-step condition. If no candidate improves the parent, return its feasible fallback. If there is no usable parent, the uniform vector is always a valid fallback for every n in [1,999]. Do not infer global optimality from local termination.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

Inside the generated program, validate the selected dimension and parent values, validate every candidate’s shape, finiteness, box bounds, and mass before it can be selected, and jointly restore feasibility by capped-simplex projection or the explicitly bounded LP-step repair. Implement the exact evaluator score as max(np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full'))*(2.0/n), including all 2n−1 full-correlation values. Lower is better. Invalid candidates receive infinity and cannot replace a valid incumbent.

Keep an exact-scored feasible fallback before starting any search. Store copies of improvements, catch failures per start or hop, and never overwrite a better candidate with a worse one. At finalization reproject, revalidate, and recompute the exact score from the returned h_values; use the fallback and then the uniform vector if recovery is needed. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level and return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values one-dimensional and finite, 0≤h_values[i]≤1, sum(h_values)=n_points/2 within floating-point tolerance, c5_bound equal to the exact formula, and n_points an integer. Do not print, perform filesystem or network I/O, or rely on calculations performed while composing the source.
